addressed-iarc-060.title: Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks
addressed-iarc-060.summary: Completeness requires regularity along the attribution path, and symmetry alone does not uniquely select integrated gradients. Later independent work gives a corrected gradient theorem and a stronger characterization with affine scale invariance.

checks.location: Proposition 1 asserts completeness under ambient almost-everywhere differentiability with the stated footnote; Theorem 1 asserts that integrated gradients is the unique symmetry-preserving path method.
checks.claim: Proposition 1 asserts completeness under ambient almost-everywhere differentiability with the stated footnote; Theorem 1 asserts that integrated gradients is the unique symmetry-preserving path method.
checks.explanation: Continuity and almost-everywhere differentiability in the ambient input space do not justify integrating a gradient along a particular path. The uniqueness argument has a separate gap: symmetry constrains a path method only when symmetric coordinates agree at both endpoints. It leaves the method free to choose other paths for other endpoint pairs.
checks.demonstration:
For completeness, extend the Cantor staircase $C:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ constantly outside the interval. This function is continuous and has derivative zero almost everywhere, yet $C(1)-C(0)=1$. Along the one-dimensional segment, integrating its almost-everywhere derivative gives $0$, contradicting the stated completeness identity. Absolute continuity, which would rule out this example, is not among the stated assumptions. Ambient Lipschitz continuity alone also leaves a path issue: $F(u,v)=\max(u,v)$ is Lipschitz, but its classical gradient is undefined at every point of the diagonal segment.

For uniqueness, work in two dimensions. Use the straight path from $p$ to $q$ whenever $p_1=p_2$ and $q_1=q_2$. For all other endpoint pairs, use
$$\gamma_1(t)=p_1+(q_1-p_1)t,\qquad \gamma_2(t)=p_2+(q_2-p_2)\left[t+\tfrac14t(1-t)\right].$$
Both coordinates are monotone, since the second time parameter has derivative $\tfrac54-\tfrac12t>0$. Whenever the original symmetry premise applies, the rule chooses the straight path, so symmetric variables receive equal attributions. For $p=(0,0)$, $q=(1,2)$ and the smooth symmetric function $F(u,v)=uv$, the curved path instead yields
$$A_1=\int_0^1\gamma_2(t)\gamma_1'(t)\,dt=\tfrac{13}{12},\qquad A_2=\int_0^1\gamma_1(t)\gamma_2'(t)\,dt=\tfrac{11}{12}.$$
Integrated gradients gives $(1,1)$. Thus this is a different, symmetry-preserving path attribution method, even with smooth monotone paths.
checks.repair:
For completeness, require $F$ to be Lipschitz on a neighborhood of the path and differentiable at $\gamma(t)$ for almost every $t$, with $\gamma$ continuously differentiable. Then $F\circ\gamma$ is absolutely continuous, and the chain rule gives
$$\sum_i A_i=\int_0^1\nabla F(\gamma(t))\cdot\gamma'(t)\,dt=F(\gamma(1))-F(\gamma(0)).$$
This is the corrected gradient theorem in [Lerma and Lucas, Proposition 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.13533v1).

For the symmetry result, retain the valid assertion that integrated gradients preserves symmetry and remove uniqueness under symmetry alone. Lundstrom and Razaviyayn give a stronger characterization in JMLR 26(177), May 2025, using an additional axiom: invariance of attributions under independent affine changes of input units. If $T$ rescales and shifts input coordinates, require $A(x,x^\prime,F)=A(Tx,Tx^\prime,F\circ T^{-1})$. [Lundstrom and Razaviyayn, Theorem 8](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume26/23-0671/23-0671.pdf) proves uniqueness among monotone path methods satisfying symmetry and affine scale invariance, on its stated class of real-analytic functions and finite networks built from analytic and ReLU layers, restricted to the domain where integrated gradients is defined. These are corrections by later authors, rather than an erratum by the original authors. Affine normalization brings the changing coordinates to common endpoints; symmetry then forces their path to follow the diagonal, up to a reparameterization that leaves the integrals unchanged.
checks.scope: The Cantor example refutes the general regularity claim; it is not a finite ReLU network. The diagonal $\max$ example shows why pathwise differentiability must be checked even for Lipschitz neural functions. The uniqueness counterexample uses a polynomial $F$ and smooth monotone paths, so it does not rely on nondifferentiability.
checks.title: Completeness needs path regularity, and symmetry alone does not identify integrated gradients
checks.claimContext: Proposition 1 asserts completeness when $F$ is differentiable almost everywhere; footnote 1 adds continuity and an almost-everywhere condition on its partial derivatives. Theorem 1 separately claims that integrated gradients is the unique symmetry-preserving path method.
checks.contextBefore: Integrated gradients integrates the coordinate gradients of $F$ along the straight segment from a baseline $x^\prime$ to an input $x$. A path method replaces that segment with a smooth path having the same endpoints.
checks.whyItMatters: Completeness accounts for the change in the model output only when the path integral obeys the gradient theorem. The corrected assumptions state when that identity holds. The stronger uniqueness result identifies the additional affine-invariance requirement needed beyond symmetry.
checks.verificationNote: The two claims need the stated regularity and axiomatic corrections; the corrected guarantees preserve the integrated-gradients method.
checks.checkedLocation: Proposition 1 and footnote 1, PDF p.3; symmetry definition and Theorem 1, p.5; Appendix A, p.10

relatedSources.summary: Directly identifies the completeness and path-uniqueness defects and supplies a corrected gradient theorem.

relatedSources.label: Lundstrom and Razaviyayn: Four Axiomatic Characterizations of the Integrated Gradients Attribution Method
relatedSources.summary: Section 4.2 and Appendix A confirm that symmetry alone is insufficient. Theorem 8 adds affine scale invariance to a characterization among monotone path methods.

addressed-iarc-060.issueTitle: The stated completeness assumptions and path-uniqueness claim need correction
addressed-iarc-060.plainExplanation: Almost-everywhere differentiability in the ambient space is insufficient for the stated completeness result along a chosen path. The symmetry definition also leaves paths unconstrained when the symmetric coordinates differ at an endpoint, so it does not establish a unique path method. Lerma and Lucas identify both problems and give precise replacements. Integrated gradients retains its completeness guarantee when the required path regularity holds.

checks.demonstration:
Write \(s=\max\{0,1-S[w_1\Delta+w_2(1-R)+w_3U]\}\). 

For a concrete negative excess, let the original verdict be Unsafe with probability \(9/10\), while the rewritten-policy verdict is always Unsafe. Independent original-prompt reruns disagree with probability \(2(9/10)(1/10)=9/50\), whereas the original and rewritten verdicts disagree with probability \(1/10\). Equation 1 therefore gives \(\Delta=-2/25\). With \(R=1\), \(U=0\), \(w_1=0.4\) and \(S=5\), the formula gives \(s=29/25>1\). These flips can be placed on ambiguous items so that \(U=0\). 

More generally \(\Delta\in[-1,1]\), so the score is bounded above by \(1+Sw_1\); this is a finite upper bound. Theorem 1 restricts \(\Delta\) to \([0,1]\), excluding this example.

checks.location: Appendix B.7, Proposition 3 (Ensemble lower bound) and its Proof; cached text lines 1217-1238
checks.claim: That conditional independence of the K flip events given the item is enough to bound the majority-vote ensemble's unreasonable-flip probability by C(K,ceil(K/2)) * ubar^ceil(K/2), where ubar is the mean of the unconditional marginal flip probabilities u_k.
checks.explanation: Judges can be conditionally independent and still fail together on the same difficult items. Averaging conditional products is not the same as multiplying the unconditional averages.
checks.demonstration:
Let an item be difficult with probability \(q=1/10\). All three judges flip deterministically on difficult items and never flip on the others. Conditional on each item, the three constant indicators are mutually independent. 

Each unconditional marginal is \(u_k=q\), and the majority also flips with probability \(q\). Thus \(u_{\mathrm{ens}}=1/10>3/100=3\bar u^2\). 

The proof incorrectly replaces \(\mathbb E[\prod_{k\in A}p_k(X)]\) by \(\prod_{k\in A}\mathbb E[p_k(X)]\).
checks.repair: Assume unconditional independence if that is justified, or retain the item distribution in the bound. With \(r=\lceil K/2\rceil\) and \(\bar p(X)=K^{-1}\sum_kp_k(X)\), the conditional union bound and Maclaurin’s inequality give \(u_{\mathrm{ens}}\le\binom Kr\mathbb E[\bar p(X)^r]\). Replacing this moment by \((\mathbb E\bar p(X))^r\) needs an additional condition; conditional independence alone is insufficient.
checks.scope: The proposition’s population-level ensemble guarantee is false under its stated conditional-independence assumption. This counterexample concerns the theorem, rather than the measured performance of the evaluated judges.

checks.claimContext: The pipeline converts a symbolic maintenance rule into a question whose displayed conditions should form a complete trigger scenario. In Figure 3, the source rule requires either the heating valve or preheat valve to be open above 10%. The generated question retains the running state, one temperature branch, the drained flag and duration, but neither valve condition.
checks.demonstration:
Let $A$ denote the running AHU, $B$ the displayed outdoor-temperature difference condition, $H$ an open heating valve above $10\%$, $P$ an open preheat valve above $10\%$, $F$ the drained flag, and $T$ the two-hour requirement. The generated question supplies
$$Q=A\land B\land F\land T.$$
The source rule additionally requires $H\lor P$, independently of its temperature disjunction. Thus, on the temperature branch selected in the question, its trigger condition is
$$R_B=Q\land(H\lor P).$$
Keep the AHU running, the temperature difference at $6^{\circ}\mathrm F$, the drained flag at $1$, and both valves at $0\%$ for two hours. All conditions in $Q$ hold, but $H\lor P$ is false, so the source rule does not trigger. Adding $H$ to the question gives a complete conjunction, $Q\land H$, which does imply the source rule.
checks.whyItMatters: The example recommends a source-rule action from conditions that need not activate that rule. Restoring the missing predicate repairs the illustrated implication; the general DNF construction is unaffected.
checks.repair: Add a valve condition to the question panel, such as heating valve $>10\%$, so that the displayed conditions form a complete DNF conjunction. The preheat-valve branch can instead be used in a separate example. Keep the two-hour requirement and align the displayed rule tree with the chosen conjunction.

checks.claim: Table 14 gives o1 means $1.87$ and $4.55$ with change $2.70$, alongside summaries across the displayed models.
checks.explanation: The o1 row gives $4.55-1.87=2.68$, rather than $2.70$, and ordinary rounding cannot reconcile those values. The reported summary means can be reproduced by excluding o1, but that cohort is not identified. The displayed standard deviations also differ from the usual unweighted summaries of all $23$ rows.
checks.scope: The discrepancies concern row arithmetic and cohort labels in Table 14. The standard-deviation calculation uses the usual unweighted across-model definition. A different cohort or weighting requires an explicit definition; the underlying responses are not determined by these summaries.
checks.claimContext: Table 14 reports 23 model rows with a core mean, a Pro mean, their change $\Delta$, and summary rows labeled Mean and SD across models. For o1, the displayed means are $1.87$ and $4.55$, but the change is $2.70$.
checks.demonstration:
The displayed difference is $4.55-1.87=2.68$. If both means were rounded to the nearest $0.01$, their unrounded difference would lie between $2.670$ and $2.690$. A value displayed as $2.70$ would instead lie between $2.695$ and $2.705$. The intervals do not meet. Thus ordinary display rounding cannot reconcile that row.

For the 23 displayed model means, the Pro mean is $4.2826087$ and the mean displayed change is $2.4417391$, rather than the reported $4.27$ and $2.43$. Excluding o1 gives $4.2704545$ and $2.4300000$, which explains both summary means to display precision. This is a plausible 22-model cohort explanation, not evidence that such a cohort was intended.

The Pro population and sample SDs across the 23 printed model means are $0.1438362$ and $0.1470689$, respectively. Let $x$ be the vector of printed model means, $y$ their unrounded values, $n=23$, and $P=I-\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}/n$, where $I$ is the identity matrix and $\mathbf1$ is the all-ones vector. The sample SD is $s(x)=\|Px\|_2/\sqrt{n-1}$. If every cell differs by at most $0.005$, then

$$|s(y)-s(x)|\le\frac{\|P(y-x)\|_2}{\sqrt{n-1}}\le0.005\sqrt{\frac{23}{22}}\approx0.0051124.$$

Consequently the unrounded sample SD is below $0.152182$, too small to round to $0.16$ under nearest rounding. Population SD has an even smaller upper bound. The corresponding sample SD across the $23$ displayed changes is $0.1386183$ and its upper bound is $0.143731$, below the $0.145$ needed to round to $0.15$.
checks.whyItMatters: The estimated shift in semantic rank depends on using the same model cohort and arithmetic in each summary.
checks.repair: Use one declared model cohort, define $\Delta_i=\mu_{i,\mathrm{Pro}}-\mu_{i,\mathrm{core}}$, and recompute the row changes and summaries from unrounded model means. For the printed 23-row values, o1’s difference is $2.68$, the Pro mean rounds to $4.28$, and the mean change rounds to $2.44$. A weighted summary or a 22-model summary may be reported if its weights or membership are stated explicitly; it should not be labeled as the ordinary summary of all 23 rows.
checks.title: Table 14’s row changes and summary statistics need reconciliation

checks.claim: Appendix B.2 reports confidence intervals for the main leaderboard using its existing per-question correctness data.
checks.explanation: GPT-5 core Macro is $65.89\%$ in Table 2 and $65.26\%$ in Table 17; Llama-3.1-8B Pro Micro is $12.89\%$ and $12.83\%$. Neither pair represents one point estimate rounded to the stated precision. Wilson recentering cannot explain the lower Micro value either: below $50\%$, the Wilson center moves upward.
checks.scope: The same underlying Micro proportion cannot yield both displayed values by rounding, or yield the lower value through Wilson recentering. The Macro comparison additionally depends on the stated per-asset centering convention; the printed tables alone do not identify which saved accuracy is correct.
checks.claimContext: Appendix B.2 says Table 17 adds confidence intervals to every cell of the main leaderboard using the existing per-question correctness data. Its accuracy entries differ from Table 2 for GPT-5 core Macro and Llama-3.1-8B Pro Micro.
checks.demonstration: The differences are $65.89-65.26=0.63$ and $12.89-12.83=0.06$ percentage points. Two entries rounded from one value to the nearest $0.01$ percentage point cannot differ by these amounts. For the Micro cell, let $\hat p$ be the observed proportion, $n>0$ the common question count, and $z>0$ the normal quantile used for a Wilson interval. Its center is $c=(\hat p+z^2/(2n))/(1+z^2/n)$, so $c-\hat p=z^2(1/2-\hat p)/(n+z^2)>0$ when $\hat p<1/2$. Thus recentering $12.89\%$ cannot produce $12.83\%$. Macro averages per-asset quantities: a change from an average of raw proportions to an average of Wilson centers could move it downward. The Macro discrepancy therefore requires the point-estimate convention and per-asset inputs to be reconciled, rather than an assumption that these two conventions coincide.
checks.whyItMatters: A leaderboard and its uncertainty table need consistent accuracy estimates before readers can compare models and intervals.
checks.repair: Use the same saved evaluation and the same point-estimate definition in both tables, then recompute the intervals. Label Wilson centers explicitly if they are displayed instead of observed accuracies. For a different checkpoint or question subset, state the difference and identify its table cells. Reconcile the two Micro entries against the correctness counts; rounding and ordinary Wilson recentering do not explain them.

review-neurips-2026-148345.title: Intrinsic Muon: Spectral Optimization on Riemannian Matrix Manifolds

checks.claim: Rank-k partial polar with k singular values tau solves KyFan-k ball LMO.
checks.explanation: The proposed matrix has $k$ singular values equal to $\tau$, so its Ky Fan norm is $k\tau$. It is infeasible for $k>1$ and need not maximize the objective even at $k=1$. The same paragraph reverses the endpoint norms and assigns this ball the radius of its dual ball. These are errors in the Ky Fan extension.
checks.demonstration:
Use the Euclidean matrix space $\mathbb R^{2\times2}$ with its Frobenius metric, an explicitly included special case of the framework. Let $H=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$, $k=2$, and $\tau=1$. The printed rule gives $Z^*=I_2$, whereas
$$\|I_2\|_{(2)}=2>1.$$
The feasible matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ attains objective $2$. Dividing the printed candidate by $k$ only gives objective $3/2$, so rescaling alone does not repair the oracle. At the other endpoint, $k=1$, the printed rank-one candidate attains $2$ while the feasible matrix $I_2$ attains $3$.

To identify the correct optimizer, write the singular values of $H$ as $\sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_d\geq0$. Von Neumann's trace inequality reduces the problem to maximizing $\sum_i\sigma_i z_i$ over sorted nonnegative singular values $z$ with $\sum_{i=1}^k z_i\leq\tau$. Define $z_{d+1}=0$ and, for $1\leq m\leq d$,
$$v_m=\frac{1}{\min(m,k)}(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{m},0,\ldots,0),\qquad a_m=\min(m,k)(z_m-z_{m+1}).$$
Then $z=\sum_m a_m v_m$, $a_m\geq0$, and $\sum_m a_m=\sum_{i=1}^k z_i\leq\tau$. Thus $z/\tau$ is a convex combination of $0,v_1,\ldots,v_d$. For $m\leq k$, the objective at $v_m$ is at most $\sigma_1$; for $m\geq k$, it is at most $\sum_i\sigma_i/k$. The vectors $v_1$ and $v_d$ attain these respective bounds. Consequently,
$$\max_{\|Z\|_{(k)}\leq\tau}\langle Z,H\rangle=\tau\max\left(\sigma_1,\frac{\sum_i\sigma_i}{k}\right).$$
This agrees with the paper's displayed dual norm but contradicts its proposed maximizer.
checks.repair:
For the Euclidean single-matrix problem, set $Z^*=0$ when $H=0$. Otherwise let $s=\operatorname{rank}(H)$ and $P_H=\sum_{i=1}^{s}u_iv_i^\top$, the polar factor supported on the nonzero singular subspaces. An exact oracle is
$$Z^*=\begin{cases}\tau u_1v_1^\top,&\sigma_1\geq\displaystyle\frac{\sum_i\sigma_i}{k},\\[4pt]\displaystyle\frac{\tau}{k}P_H,&\sigma_1<\displaystyle\frac{\sum_i\sigma_i}{k}.\end{cases}$$
The first branch is feasible and attains $\tau\sigma_1$. In the second branch, $\sum_i\sigma_i>k\sigma_1$ implies $s>k$, so its $k$ largest singular values are all $\tau/k$. It is feasible and attains $\tau\sum_i\sigma_i/k$. Choosing the first branch at equality also gives the optimum. No arbitrary completion of the polar factor on a nullspace is needed.

The corresponding squared Frobenius radius is
$$C=\sup_{\|Z\|_{(k)}\leq\tau}\frac{\|Z\|_F^2}{\tau^2}=\max\left(1,\frac{d}{k^2}\right).$$
The convex-combination representation above bounds the squared norm by the largest $\|v_m\|_2^2=m/\min(m,k)^2$. This is $\max(1,d/k^2)$ and is attained by $v_1$ or $v_d$. Both branches matter: $(d,k)=(3,2)$ gives $C=1$, while $(d,k)=(9,2)$ gives $C=9/4$. Correct the endpoint names to spectral at $k=1$ and nuclear at $k=d$.

Substituting this exact oracle and radius into Theorem 5.3 gives $\min_{t\leq T}\|H_t\|_{(k)}^\circ\leq\sqrt{2LC\Delta_0/T}$ in the Euclidean single-matrix setting, where $L$ is the theorem's smoothness constant, $\Delta_0=f(x_0)-f^*$ is its initial objective gap, and its step-size restriction is retained. A restricted tangent space must still admit the chosen oracle, and product spaces require their own block-radius calculation. The Euclidean correction does not establish those additional feasibility claims.
checks.scope: The demonstrated defect is the Ky Fan oracle and radius in Appendix C.3. The Euclidean counterexample satisfies the paper's setting. It leaves the general descent argument with a valid oracle, the separately derived spectral, Frobenius and nuclear cases, and their experiments unchallenged.

checks.claim: Eq4 is the optimal coupling for any target decomposition
checks.explanation: Opposite extreme displacements can cancel in the target marginal while leaving off-diagonal mass in their mixed coupling. For the displayed detector, increasing diagonal mass strictly increases expected log growth. The mixture is a feasible coupling, but it need not maximize the inner objective. Remark 4.2 already identifies maximal coupling as the intended construction; Equation (4) does not give that coupling for every interior target.
checks.demonstration:
Take $n=2$, $p_0=(2/5,3/5)$, and $\delta=1/10$, so $\min_v p_0(v)>\delta$. The two extreme targets are
$$q_+=p_0+\frac1{20}(1,-1),\qquad q_-=p_0-\frac1{20}(1,-1).$$
Their equal-weight average is $q=p_0$, which lies in the allowed neighborhood. Equation (4) produces, with outcome indexing rows and seed indexing columns,
$$W=\begin{pmatrix}3/8&1/40\\1/40&23/40\end{pmatrix}.$$
Both its row sums and column sums are $p_0$. The diagonal coupling $D=\operatorname{diag}(p_0)$ has the same marginals. Thus both are feasible under the theorem's exact constraints.

Set $a=1-\delta/2=19/20$ and $b=\delta/[2(n-1)]=1/20$. Equation (3) has $e^*(v,s)=a/p_0(s)$ on the diagonal and $b/p_0(s)$ off the diagonal. Since the seed marginal is fixed,
$$J(w):=\sum_{v,s}w(v,s)\log e^*(v,s)=H(p_0)+\log b+\operatorname{tr}(w)\log(a/b).$$
Here $H(p_0)=-\sum_s p_0(s)\log p_0(s)$. As $\operatorname{tr}(D)-\operatorname{tr}(W)=1/20$,
$$J(D)-J(W)=\frac{\log19}{20}>0.$$
Numerically, the two values are approximately $0.621718373$ and $0.474496424$. Therefore the mixed coupling is not an inner optimizer. This example uses an interior target; the individual extreme-target couplings do maximize diagonal mass.
checks.repair:
Use a maximal coupling for each actual target $q$. Define
$$u_v=(q(v)-p_0(v))_+,\quad z_v=(p_0(v)-q(v))_+,\quad t=\sum_vu_v=\sum_vz_v=\frac12\|q-p_0\|_1.$$
Here $(a)_+=\max(a,0)$ denotes the positive part. If $t=0$, set $w=\operatorname{diag}(p_0)$. If $t>0$, set
$$w(v,s)=\mathbf1\{v=s\}\min\{q(v),p_0(v)\}+\frac{u_vz_s}{t}.$$
The row sums are $q(v)$ and the column sums are $p_0(s)$. Since $u_vz_v=0$, its diagonal sum is $\sum_v\min\{q(v),p_0(v)\}=1-t$. Every feasible coupling has $w(v,v)\le\min\{q(v),p_0(v)\}$, so this diagonal sum is maximal.

For $a=1-\delta/2$ and $b=\delta/[2(n-1)]$, the assumption $\delta<\min_vp_0(v)\le1/n$ implies $a>b>0$. The objective derived above is therefore strictly increasing in diagonal mass. This proves optimality of the replacement for the displayed $e^*$ at every allowed $q$. It also gives
$$\inf_{\|q-p_0\|_1\le\delta}\sup_{w\in\mathcal P(p_0,q)}J(w)=H(p_0)+\left(1-\frac\delta2\right)\log a+\frac\delta2\log b.$$
The infimum is attained at $t=\delta/2$, which is feasible under the anchor assumption. Thus the fixed detector's worst-case inner growth remains the value in Equation (5). This calculation does not establish optimality over all other detectors or prove the separate stopping-time theorem.
checks.scope: The general-target coupling formula in Theorem 4.1 and Proposition A.6 fails for interior $q$ when its extreme-point decomposition cancels displacement. A maximal coupling repairs the inner optimization for the displayed $e^*$ and yields the same fixed-detector worst-case growth. The argument neither disproves nor proves the outer detector optimum or the stopping-time result.
checks.title: Mixing extreme couplings need not be optimal at an interior target
checks.whyItMatters: At an interior target, the proposed mixture can discard available log-growth efficiency even though it preserves both required marginals. The maximal coupling implements the pointwise optimum that the theorem and its comparison with speculative decoding intend.
checks.claimContext: Theorem 4.1 assumes a finite alphabet of size $n\ge2$, an anchor distribution $p_0$ with $\min_v p_0(v)>\delta>0$, and a target $q$ satisfying $\|q-p_0\|_1\le\delta$. For the displayed detector $e^*$, Equation (4) claims that any convex decomposition of $q$ into the extreme targets $q_i=p_0+(\delta/2)(\mathbf e_{v_i}-\mathbf e_{s_i})$ gives an optimal coupling through the same convex combination of their couplings. Proposition A.6 repeats this assertion.

review-neurips-2026-148620.title: Feature-Context Consistency: Unsupervised Adversarial Detection with Drift Stability on Attributed Graphs

checks.claim: Sign-corrected nonnegative coordinate covariances imply positive expected cosine alignment.
checks.explanation: Covariance weights observations by their magnitudes; cosine normalizes those magnitudes away. A few large aligned pairs can make covariance positive while most pairs point in opposite directions.
checks.demonstration:
Consider a graph of $40$ legitimate nodes in $20$ disjoint undirected pairs. Eighteen pairs have scalar features $(1,-1)$; the other two have $(10,10)$ and $(-10,-10)$. Each node’s raw context is its partner’s feature. Uniform sampling over nodes gives zero means and
$$\operatorname{Cov}(x,c)=\frac{-36+4\cdot100}{40}=9.1>0.$$
Both variances are $10.9$, so Pearson correlation is positive and the sign correction is $+1$. Yet $36$ nodes have cosine $-1$ and only four have cosine $+1$:
$$\mathbb E[\cos(x,c)]=\frac{-36+4}{40}=-0.8.$$
All features and contexts are nonzero and bounded. The paper-linked implementation also returns sign $+1$ for these exact inputs.
checks.repair:
Treat positive population mean cosine as a separate assumption and measure the cosine itself when assessing a dataset. A sufficient distributional condition can also be stated explicitly: if $\mathbb E x=\mathbb E c=0$ and $\|x\|_2=a$, $\|c\|_2=b$ are positive constants, then
$$\mathbb E[\cos(x,c)]=\frac{\sum_d\operatorname{Cov}(x_d,c_d)}{ab}.$$
Under these additional conditions, nonnegative coordinate covariances with at least one strictly positive term imply positive mean cosine. A finite training estimate alone is not a population lower bound.
checks.scope: The counterexample disproves the justification in Remark 5.1. The separation theorem is explicitly conditional on Assumption 1; positive population mean cosine must be supplied independently of the coordinate-sign correction.
checks.title: Positive coordinate covariance does not imply positive mean cosine
checks.claimContext: The context vector is the mean feature vector of a node’s neighbors, with each coordinate multiplied by the sign of its training-set Pearson correlation. Remark 5.1 uses the resulting nonnegative coordinate covariances to justify the population assumption $\mathbb E[\cos(x,c)]\ge\rho_0>0$.
checks.whyItMatters: Sign correction can improve a correlation statistic without establishing the geometric alignment required by the detection guarantee.
checks.checkedLocation: Remark 5.1 and Assumption 1, PDF page 5; signed neighbor mean in Equation (1)

checks.claim: There exists positive delta strictly smaller than all displayed edge-minus-subset valuation gaps.
checks.explanation: An admissible tied comparison contributes a zero gap, so the printed positive parameter need not exist. Deleting zero terms is not by itself a reduction proof: strict-envy comparisons and equality cases must be checked separately, and the gap set must cover the actual original bundles used later.
checks.demonstration: Take a unit-valued triangle with \(e=(i,j)\) and \(f=(i,h)\). The subset \(J=\{f\}\) satisfies the displayed weak endpoint comparisons: \(v_i(J)=v_i(e)=1\) and \(v_j(J)=0\le v_j(e)=1\). Its endpoint gaps are zero and one. Thus the minimum in the printed choice can be zero and no \(\delta>0\) satisfies it. Tied positive valuations are allowed by the graph model; no generic-position assumption removes this example.
checks.repair:
Let \(\widehat M\) denote the original edge set. Define \[G_+=\{v_i(e)-v_i(J)>0:\ e\in\widehat M,\ i\in e,\ J\subseteq\widehat M\setminus\{e\}\}.\] Choose \(0<\delta<\min(\{1\}\cup G_+)\), which is possible for a finite instance, including when \(G_+\) is empty. This set covers all strict original comparisons without relying on the ambiguous \(Z(e)\) definition. For rational input values, let \(D\) be the product of their positive denominators and take \(\delta=1/(2D)\). Every positive original gap is at least \(1/D\), and the bit length of \(D\) is at most the sum of the input denominator bit lengths, so the choice has polynomial encoding length without enumerating subsets.

Here is the required tie-aware transfer argument, conditional on the gadget orienting every connecting edge toward its original vertex. Write \(A_i\) for the original bundle and \(X_i\) for that bundle plus its connecting edge, when present. If the original orientation is \(\mathrm{EF}(k-1)\mathrm{X}\), any removal of \(k\) edges from \(X_j\) removes at least \(k-1\) old edges. For a distinct original observer \(i\), the connecting edge of \(j\) has value zero, and \(v_i(X_i)\ge v_i(A_i)\). The old weak inequality therefore proves the new one, including equality. Bundles too small for such a removal give no obstruction.

Conversely, suppose an old comparison fails after removing \(k-1\) edges from \(A_j\). Because the graph is simple, the remaining positive value to \(i\) is its unique edge \(e=(i,j)\), and \(v_i(e)>v_i(A_i)\). The envied bundle contains at least \(k\) old edges, so \(j\) receives a connecting edge. Remove that edge together with the \(k-1\) old edges. New \(\mathrm{EF}k\mathrm{X}\) would require \(v_i(A_i)+b_i\delta\ge v_i(e)\), where \(b_i\in\{0,1\}\); the positive-gap choice makes this impossible. If \(v_i(A_i)=v_i(e)\), there is already no old envy, so equality requires no strict gap. This proves the transfer for all pairs of original vertices. The full hardness reduction must additionally establish the enhancer/funnel forcing property and the extension’s gadget-pair inequalities; those are separate obligations from selecting \(\delta\).

checks.claim: Constant Frobenius normalization makes peak similarity exactly duration-invariant for spectrally diffuse content.
checks.explanation: A bound that does not depend on duration need not be attained at every duration. Fixing the sum of squared frequency coefficients fixes the Frobenius norm; it does not fix their sum or the largest attainable similarity.
checks.demonstration:
Work in the continuous event-sampling limit used in the appendix. Take $d_{\mathrm{rope}}=4$, the two standard frequencies $(1,0.01)$, and unit vectors
$$q=k=(1,0,1,0)/\sqrt2.$$
The two frequency blocks have equal amplitude $1/2$. With $\operatorname{sinc}(u)=\sin(u)/u$, the averaging factors are $\operatorname{sinc}(\theta_nL/2)$. At zero duration the similarity peak is one.

At $L=2\pi$, the first factor is zero and the second is positive. Frobenius normalization gives
$$\beta(L)=\frac{\sqrt2}{\operatorname{sinc}(0.01\pi)}.$$
Only the slow block remains, so its cosine reaches a peak
$$\max_t s(t;2\pi)=\beta(L)\frac{\operatorname{sinc}(0.01\pi)}2=\frac1{\sqrt2}.$$
The normalized squared Frobenius norm is still four. Thus the peak changes despite equal energy across all blocks and a slow-frequency product $0.01L\ll1$.

If approximate peak stability is needed, state and prove quantitative conditions on the frequency weights, phases and duration range, or report it as a measured property of a specified query–key distribution. checks.claim: Growth upper bounds imply strict monotonicity of marginal regret and a unique optimum.
checks.explanation: Upper bounds on total regret do not make the actual marginal-regret curves monotone. Appendix A.5 infers that shape from the powers appearing in the bounds, so its uniqueness argument requires an additional hypothesis. The endpoint conditions still ensure that at least one interior minimizer strictly improves on both endpoints.
checks.demonstration:
Use the continuous marginal-regret formulation in Theorem 4.6 with total dimension $d=1$. On $[0,1]$, choose
$$r_{\rm RL}(h)=1-\cos(5\pi h),\qquad r_{\rm DM}(h)=1.$$
Both marginals are continuous and nonnegative. The strict boundary conditions hold because $r_{\rm RL}(0)=0<1=r_{\rm DM}(0)$ and $r_{\rm RL}(1)=2>1=r_{\rm DM}(1)$. The handover objective is
$$\mathcal L(\tau)=\int_0^\tau r_{\rm RL}(h)\,dh+\int_\tau^1r_{\rm DM}(h)\,dh=1-\frac{\sin(5\pi\tau)}{5\pi}.$$
Since sine is at most one, the global minimum is $1-1/(5\pi)$, attained at all three points $\tau=0.1,0.5,0.9$. The claimed uniqueness therefore fails.

The example also satisfies strengthened growth interpretations. Extend the RL total regret to nonnegative $h$ by
$$R_{\rm RL}(h)=h-\frac{\sin(5\pi h)}{5\pi}+(h-1)_+^3,$$
where $(h-1)_+=\max(h-1,0)$. It agrees with the preceding integral on $[0,1]$, is $O(h^3)$ near zero and $\Theta(h^3)$ at infinity. Extend the DM total regret by
$$R_{\rm DM}(u)=\begin{cases}u,&0\le u\le1,\\2\sqrt u-1,&u\ge1.\end{cases}$$
This has $O(\sqrt u)$ growth and still gives $R_{\rm DM}(1-\tau)=1-\tau$ on the instance. Thus genuine superlinear RL growth and square-root DM growth do not force a single crossing of the marginal regrets.

The strict boundary signs do exclude both endpoints from being minimizers: the objective decreases immediately to the right of zero and increases immediately to the left of one. Continuity on the compact interval therefore still gives an interior global minimizer strictly better than either endpoint. The counterexample refutes uniqueness, not that existence and strict-improvement conclusion. It concerns the implication from the scalar regret assumptions and does not purport to instantiate the trained neural policies.
checks.repair: Add continuity and strict increase of $g(\tau)=r_{\rm RL}(\tau)-r_{\rm DM}(\tau)$ as explicit assumptions. The existing opposite endpoint signs then give exactly one zero of $g$. Since $\mathcal L'(\tau)=g(\tau)$ changes from negative to positive there, that zero is the unique global minimizer. Alternatively, remove uniqueness: continuity and the original strict boundary signs already imply an interior global minimizer strictly better than either endpoint. Regret-growth envelopes alone establish neither the new monotonicity assumption nor an exact-optimum guarantee for the practical entropy or disagreement trigger.
checks.scope: The gap concerns Theorem 4.6 and the shape inference in Appendix A.5. Neither the original growth bounds nor the repaired theorem establishes that the practical trigger identifies the optimum for a trained solver.
checks.claimContext: Theorem 4.6 models hybrid regret as the accumulated RL regret before a handover plus DM regret afterward. It claims a unique optimal trigger from regret-growth bounds and opposite marginal-regret inequalities at the two endpoints.
checks.whyItMatters: The endpoint conditions guarantee an interior minimizer, but uniqueness needs an explicit shape assumption. The counterexample preserves the existence and strict hybrid-improvement conclusion within the stated additive regret model.
checks.title: Regret growth bounds do not imply a unique handover point
checks.verificationNote: In arXiv v1, Theorem 4.6 and Appendix A.5 support an interior minimizer under the endpoint conditions. Uniqueness requires the additional strict-monotonicity condition stated in the repair.
checks.checkedLocation: Theorem 4.6; Lemmas 4.4–4.5; Appendix A.5

checks.location: Appendix B Normalized GED after Eq.5
checks.claim: GED divided by larger edge count always lies in [0,1].
checks.explanation: Two graphs can require both edge deletions and edge insertions. Their sum can exceed either graph's edge count, even after optimizing the vertex correspondence.
checks.demonstration:
Take six vertices. Let \(G_1=K_{1,5}\) be a five-edge star and let \(G_2\) be a three-edge perfect matching. All star edges share one vertex, while matching degree is one, so any vertex correspondence preserves at most one edge. Preserving one is possible. Thus

\[\operatorname{GED}(G_1,G_2)=5+3-2\cdot1=6,\qquad\frac{\operatorname{GED}}{\max(5,3)}=\frac65>1.\]

A partial correspondence cannot preserve more edges; unmatched vertices add nonnegative costs. Under the printed node-and-edge cost convention, removing a vertex does not make its incident edge deletions free. Both graphs can be oriented acyclically and padded with five isolated vertices to have eleven vertices.
checks.repair:
For equal vertex counts, retain free vertex relabeling and normalize by the sum of edge counts:

\[d_{\mathrm{sum}}(G_1,G_2)=\frac{\operatorname{GED}(G_1,G_2)}{|E_1|+|E_2|}.\]

Define \(d_{\mathrm{sum}}=0\) when both edge sets are empty. Deleting every source edge and inserting every target edge is an admissible edit path, so \(0\le\operatorname{GED}\le|E_1|+|E_2|\), proving \(d_{\mathrm{sum}}\in[0,1]\). The witness becomes \(3/4\). For different vertex counts, a separate universal upper bound is \(|V_1|+|V_2|+|E_1|+|E_2|\), the cost of deleting and recreating the entire graph. The endpoint interpretation must match the chosen normalization.
checks.scope: This corrects the general range statement for the graph metric. It does not contradict the paper's particular comparison \(\operatorname{GED}=2\), normalized to approximately \(2/13\), or its empirical data-coherence results.
checks.title: The normalized graph edit distance can exceed one
checks.claimContext: Appendix B assigns unit cost to each node or edge insertion/deletion and zero substitution cost. After projecting to undirected graphs, it states that dividing the minimum edit cost by the larger edge count always gives a value in \([0,1]\).
checks.whyItMatters: A bounded graph distance needs a denominator that covers the allowed edit costs. Changing this normalization gives a bounded comparison without changing the reported pair of graphs.

Under the assumption $p({\bm{t}}_{1}^{\text{src}})\geq q\,p^{\text{tool}}$ , applying $f$ to both sides gives $1-(1-p({\bm{t}}_{1}^{\text{src}}))^{N}\geq 1-(1-q\,p^{\text{tool}})^{N}$ . Strictness follows whenever $p({\bm{t}}_{1}^{\text{src}})>q\,p^{\text{tool}}$ and $q\,p^{\text{tool}}\in(0,1)$ . The mechanism is $q\to 1$ by construction: resampling eliminates raw’s wasted $(1-q)$ fraction of non-tool rollouts, so the baseline threshold is $q\,p^{\text{tool}}$ rather than $p^{\text{tool}}$ .
checks.contextAfter: By the definition of $p^{\text{tool}}$ as the conditional expectation over the tool-committed prefix distribution $\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid{\bm{x}},\,{\bm{t}}_{1}\in\mathcal{T})$ , $\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{t}}_{1}}[p({\bm{t}}_{1})]=p^{\text{tool}}>q\,p^{\text{tool}}$ whenever $q<1$ , so the expected prefix lies strictly above the Proposition 1 threshold. checks.demonstration:
Let $m_i\ge0$ be the MSE of window $i$ and $w_i\ge0$ weights summing to one. Jensen’s inequality gives
$$\sum_i w_i\sqrt{m_i}\le\sqrt{\sum_iw_i m_i}.$$
Here $\sqrt{13.525}=3.677635$, while $3.753^2=14.085009$. Even rounding cannot explain a matched comparison, since $3.7525^2=14.08125625>13.5255$.

A hypothetical paired subset uses two equally weighted TimeClaw windows with MSEs $14.085009$ and $12.964991$. Table 4's full mean is $13.525$; Table 8's first-window RMSE is $3.753$. Give GPT-5.4 MSE $20.984$ on both windows. Its full MSE remains $20.984$ and its paired-subset RMSE rounds to the reported $4.581$, so the matching baseline does not establish sample identity. The source does not say this subset was used; the example shows exactly what evidence is missing.

checks.location: Assumption 1.13, line 300; Theorems 3.4/3.7 and Appendix C.2.2 stepsize passage
checks.claim: A bounded deterministic schedule sampled at k/d suffices for SGD and the continuous SDE/PDE to have the same algebraically accurate learning curves.
checks.explanation: Discrete SGD samples $\gamma$ at times $k/d$; homogenized SGD integrates $\gamma$ and $\gamma^2$ over time. Boundedness alone gives no agreement between those operations. Appendix C.2 interpolates the sampled coefficients, then replaces them with the continuous coefficients without bounding the difference across the full interval. A bounded schedule can make that difference persist, and even a continuous schedule can make it decay more slowly than every power of $d^{-1}$.
checks.demonstration:
Take $K=I_d$, $\psi(u,v)=u$, $f(r_1,r_2)=(r_1-r_2)^2/2$, $u_0=v_0=0$, and $\beta^*=b_d\mathbf 1$ with $b_d=1/\log(d+1)$. The linear map is allowed by Assumption 1.8 through $\mathcal Q=0$, $l=(1,0)$, and $c=0$. For these choices, $h(B)=(B_{11}-B_{12}-B_{21}+B_{22})/2$, $I=2h$, and $\mathcal U=\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ satisfy the stated regularity assumptions.

Choose the bounded measurable schedule $\gamma(t)=\mathbf 1_{\mathbb Q}(t)$. Every grid value $\gamma(k/d)$ is $1$, whereas both the drift integral and quadratic variation in Equation (14) vanish. Thus homogenized SGD stays at its initial point and has constant risk $R_0=b_d^2/2$. With $e_k=u_k-\beta^*$, the actual SGD update is
$$e_{k+1}=\left(I_d-\frac{a_{k+1}a_{k+1}^{\top}}d\right)e_k,\qquad R_k=\frac{\|e_k\|^2}{2d}.$$
Gaussian moments give
$$\mathbb E[R_{k+1}\mid e_k]=\left(1-\frac1d+\frac2{d^2}\right)R_k,\qquad \frac{\mathbb E[R_d]}{R_0}\longrightarrow e^{-1}.$$
Since the risk is nonnegative, Markov's inequality gives $\mathbb P(R_d\leq0.8R_0)\geq1-\mathbb E[R_d]/(0.8R_0)\to1-e^{-1}/0.8>0.54$. On that event the risk difference from homogenized SGD is at least $0.2R_0=1/[10\log^2(d+1)]$, which exceeds $Cd^{-\varepsilon}$ eventually for every fixed $C$ and $\varepsilon>0$. If both risks were within $Cd^{-\varepsilon}$ of one deterministic curve, their difference would be at most $2Cd^{-\varepsilon}$. The lower bound above rules this out with probability bounded away from zero.

The coordinate bound in Assumption 3.1 does not exclude this example. With overwhelming probability, all $\lfloor Td\rfloor$ Gaussian samples have $\|a_k\|^2\leq2d$, so every residual update is a contraction. Conditional on this rotation-invariant event, the law of $e_k$ is invariant under rotations fixing $e_0$. Its component along $e_0$ contributes at most $b_d$ to each coordinate; its perpendicular component has norm at most $b_d\sqrt d$ and a uniform spherical direction. A union bound over coordinates and times therefore bounds the probability that any $|u_{k,i}|>1$ by $\operatorname{poly}(d)e^{-c\log^2(d+1)}+\operatorname{poly}(d)e^{-cd}$. The inactive coordinates $v$ and the homogenized process stay zero. Thus one fixed coordinate bound works for every fixed time horizon.

Requiring continuity alone still leaves the algebraic rate unsupported. To see this, keep the same model and choose the single, dimension-independent schedule
$$\gamma(t)=\frac1{10}\left(1+\sum_{j\geq1}2^{-j}\cos(2\pi m_jt)\right),\qquad m_j=2^{2^j}.$$
The series converges uniformly, so $\gamma$ is continuous and lies in $[0,1/5]$. Over $[0,1]$, $\int\gamma=1/10$ and $\int\gamma^2=7/600$, hence $H=\int(-2\gamma+\gamma^2)=-113/600$. At dimensions $d_n=m_n$, every frequency with $j\geq n$ aliases to $1$ on the SGD grid. Writing $W_n=2^{1-n}$, discrete orthogonality gives grid averages $\overline\gamma=(1+W_n)/10$ and $\overline{\gamma^2}=7/600+W_n/50+W_n^2/120$. The exact Gaussian recurrence therefore gives
$$\log\frac{\mathbb E[R_{d_n}]}{R_0}=H-\frac9{50}W_n+\frac{W_n^2}{120}+O(d_n^{-1}).$$
For homogenized SGD, Itô's formula gives $\mathrm dR=(-2\gamma+\gamma^2)R\,\mathrm dt+(2\gamma/\sqrt d)R\,\mathrm dB$. Its time-one risk is $e^H R_0$ up to relative fluctuations of order $d^{-1/2}$. Applying Markov's inequality to SGD at the midpoint between its mean and $e^H R_0$ gives a risk separation of order $R_0W_n$ with probability of order $W_n$. Since $W_n=2\log 2/\log d_n$, these are logarithmic scales, incompatible with the claimed algebraic accuracy with overwhelming probability. The earlier contraction and spherical-tail argument also bounds the SGD coordinates for this schedule. For the SDE, the exact radial geometric-Brownian representation bounds the residual norm by $C_Tb_d\sqrt d$ with overwhelming probability, and each coordinate martingale has quadratic variation at most $C_Tb_d^2$ before that norm bound. Exponential martingale tails and a union bound give the same fixed coordinate bound as above.
checks.repair:
Require $\gamma$ to be Lipschitz on every bounded time interval, with its bound $\bar\gamma$ and Lipschitz constant $L_T$ independent of $d$. For the schedule sampled by SGD, write $\gamma_d(s)=\gamma(\lfloor ds\rfloor/d)$. Then, for $0\leq s\leq T$,
$$|\gamma_d(s)-\gamma(s)|\leq\frac{L_T}{d},\qquad |\gamma_d(s)^2-\gamma(s)^2|\leq\frac{2\bar\gamma L_T}{d}.$$
On the stopped domain used in Appendix C.2, the predictable drift has bounded coefficients multiplying $\gamma$ and $\gamma^2$. Integrating the displayed discrepancies therefore adds at most $C_T(1+2\bar\gamma)L_T/d$ to the remainder. Include this term when passing from Equation (90) to Proposition C.4 across the whole time interval, rather than bounding only the final fractional interval. This controls the omitted schedule error at order $d^{-1}$; constant schedules incur zero error. It repairs this coefficient replacement under the other stated hypotheses. It does not supply a new existence proof for the deterministic equation, whose solution-existence conditions must remain part of any theorem that uses it.
checks.scope: The defect concerns the schedules permitted by Assumption 1.13 and the simultaneous learning-curve guarantee in Theorem 3.7. Both examples meet the coordinate bounds in Assumption 3.1. Theorem 3.4 also requires a solution of the deterministic equation; the stochastic-curve separation above does not establish existence of that solution for an arbitrary bounded schedule.

review-neurips-2026-156782.title: Mollifier Layers: Enabling Efficient High-Order Derivatives in Inverse PDE Learning

checks.location: Section3.2 Eq7, work/text/156782.txt:158-165; Appendix A.8 Eq40, lines1288-1292; Eqs45-46, lines1320-1330
checks.claim: A C1 field that is L-Lipschitz has O(L delta) uniform first-derivative mollification bias, supporting the main O(delta+h+epsilon) guarantee and an O(sqrt(h)) consequence at delta~sqrt(h).
checks.explanation: A Lipschitz bound on $f$ controls the size of $f'$ but not its rate of variation. Derivative bias depends on the modulus of continuity of $f'$. A continuous derivative can vary like a square root near an interior point, producing bias of order $\sqrt\delta$ rather than the claimed order $\delta$.
checks.demonstration:
Set $x_0=1/2$ and choose the single fixed field
$$f(x)=\frac23\operatorname{sgn}(x-x_0)|x-x_0|^{3/2}.$$
Its derivative is $f'(x)=\sqrt{|x-x_0|}$, so $f\in C^1([0,1])$ and its field Lipschitz constant is $L=1/\sqrt2$. Normalize the smooth bump $\exp[-1/(1-s^2)]$ on $|s|<1$ to unit mass and set it to zero outside that interval. This gives an admissible nonnegative $C^\infty$ kernel.

For $0<\delta<1/2$, the convolution window around $x_0$ lies entirely inside the domain. Differentiating under the integral yields
$$\partial_xJ_\delta f(x_0)-f'(x_0)=A\sqrt\delta,\qquad A=\int_{-1}^1\rho(s)\sqrt{|s|}\,ds>0.$$
Dividing by $L\delta$ gives $A/(L\sqrt\delta)\to\infty$, so no fixed constant $C$ can make Equation (40) hold.

The same example defeats the noiseless main rate. Take centered-difference spacing $h=\delta^2$. Since $f'$ is square-root continuous, replacing the mollified derivative at $x_0$ by its centered difference changes it by at most $\sqrt h=\delta$. The leading bias remains $A\sqrt\delta$, which dominates the claimed order $\delta+h$. A normalized sampled convolution reproduces the same leading bias. Neither noise nor a boundary effect is needed.
checks.repair:
Use the derivative's modulus of continuity,
$$\omega_{f'}(t)=\sup_{|x-y|\leq t}|f'(x)-f'(y)|.$$
Differentiating the convolution and averaging gives the valid interior estimate $\|\partial_xJ_\delta f-f'\|_\infty\leq\omega_{f'}(\delta)$. If $f'$ is $M$-Lipschitz, this becomes $M\delta$; the linear-bias constant must control the derivative, not only the field.

For the grid-data theorem, state the operation explicitly. Let $g_j=f(jh)+n_j$, $|n_j|\leq\varepsilon$, and define nonnegative weights
$$w_k=\frac{\rho(kh/\delta)}{\sum_\ell\rho(\ell h/\delta)},\qquad J_\delta^hg_j=\sum_kw_kg_{j+k},$$
assuming the denominator is positive. At grid points at least $\delta+h$ from the boundary, averaging the centered-difference integral of $f'$ gives
$$\|D_0J_\delta^hg-f'\|_\infty\leq\omega_{f'}(\delta+h)+\varepsilon K_{\delta,h},\qquad K_{\delta,h}=\frac1{2h}\sum_k|w_{k-1}-w_{k+1}|.$$
The first term corrects the regularity defect. The second is the separate noise contribution. For a fixed smooth kernel and $h/\delta\to0$, it has $K_{\delta,h}=O(1/\delta)$. Thus a Lipschitz $f'$, $\delta\asymp\sqrt h$, and $\varepsilon=O(h)$ recover an $O(\sqrt h)$ interior error. Without a Lipschitz derivative, the modulus gives qualitative convergence rather than that rate; for an $n$th derivative, the corresponding argument requires $f^{(n)}$ and its modulus of continuity.
checks.scope: The defect is the quantitative regularity assumption in the derivative guarantee, already visible for zero noise and an interior point. Replacing linear bias by the derivative's modulus preserves qualitative convergence; assuming a Lipschitz first derivative restores linear bias. The normalized-grid bound also requires the separately stated bandwidth and noise conditions.
checks.title: Lipschitz continuity of a field does not give linear derivative bias
checks.claimContext: Appendix A.8 assumes a field $f\in C^1([0,1])$ that is $L$-Lipschitz and a nonnegative smooth unit-mass kernel $\rho$ supported on $[-1,1]$. Equation (40) claims linear decay of the mollified first-derivative bias as the kernel width $\delta$ decreases. This supplies the bias term in the main derivative-consistency bound:
checks.whyItMatters: The stated $C^1$ regularity supports derivative convergence but not the advertised rate. With $\delta=\sqrt h$, this fixed noiseless field has bias of order $h^{1/4}$ instead of $h^{1/2}$, so the rate cannot be recovered solely by changing the noise schedule.

checks.location: Section3.2 Eq7, work/text/156782.txt:158-165; Appendix A.8 constants line1280 and Eqs42-43 lines1300-1312
checks.claim: With only bounded observation errors |n_j|<=epsilon, the derivative error is bounded by C1 delta+C2(h+epsilon) with constants independent of bandwidth, grid spacing and noise. Appendix Eq42 additionally bounds a noisy-versus-noiseless derivative difference by Ch^2 alone.
checks.explanation: Differentiation of a mollified perturbation has a noise contribution of order $\varepsilon/\delta$. The claimed term proportional only to $\varepsilon$ misses this amplification as the smoothing window narrows. Taking the true field to be zero isolates this noise effect from any question about field regularity.
checks.demonstration:
Let $u=0$, take the interior point $x_0=1/2$, and set
$$h=\delta^2,\qquad n_\delta(x)=\sqrt\delta\sin\!\left(\frac{x-x_0}{\delta}\right),\qquad \varepsilon=\sqrt\delta.$$
Use dyadic $\delta$ so $x_0$ is a grid point. Every observed grid value obeys the allowed noise bound. For an admissible symmetric nonnegative unit-mass kernel, define
$$A=\int_{-1}^1\rho(s)\cos s\,ds\geq\cos1>0.$$
Convolution multiplies the sinusoid by $A$, so the centered difference is exactly
$$D_0J_\delta n_\delta(x_0)=A\sqrt\delta\,\frac{\sin(h/\delta)}h=A\frac{\sin\delta}{\delta^{3/2}}\sim\frac A{\sqrt\delta}.$$
The derivative error therefore diverges while the proposed upper bound tends to zero, since $\delta+h+\varepsilon\to0$.

This contradiction also holds for normalized grid convolution. Set $w_k=\rho(kh/\delta)/\sum_\ell\rho(\ell h/\delta)$ and replace $A$ by
$$A_h=\sum_kw_k\cos(kh/\delta)\geq\cos1.$$
The same centered-difference identity holds exactly. The example therefore does not depend on a continuous approximation to grid data. It also contradicts Equation (42), which bounds a noisy-versus-noiseless derivative difference by $Ch^2$ alone.
checks.repair:
Define the normalized grid convolution by $J_\delta^hg_j=\sum_kw_kg_{j+k}$, with $w_k=\rho(kh/\delta)/\sum_\ell\rho(\ell h/\delta)$ and a positive denominator. For $u\in C^1$ and grid points at least $\delta+h$ from the boundary, the corrected bound is
$$\|D_0J_\delta^hg-u'\|_\infty\leq\omega_{u'}(\delta+h)+\varepsilon K_{\delta,h},\qquad K_{\delta,h}=\frac1{2h}\sum_k|w_{k-1}-w_{k+1}|,$$
where $\omega_{u'}$ is the modulus of continuity of $u'$. Each noiseless centered difference averages $u'$ within distance $\delta+h$ of its evaluation point, giving the first term. Reindexing the noise sum gives coefficients $(w_{k-1}-w_{k+1})/(2h)$; their absolute sum is the exact operator norm on bounded noise.

For a fixed smooth kernel with $h/\delta\to0$, the normalization sum is asymptotic to $\delta/h$ and $K_{\delta,h}=O(1/\delta)$. Interior derivative consistency therefore follows from $\delta\to0$, $h/\delta\to0$, and $\varepsilon=o(\delta)$. If $u'$ is Lipschitz, choosing $\delta\asymp\sqrt h$ and $\varepsilon=O(h)$ gives error $O(\sqrt h)$. The stricter schedule $\varepsilon\asymp h^2$ suggested in Appendix A.8 also suffices with this derivative regularity, but that schedule is absent from the displayed uniform claim.
checks.scope: The example disproves the uniform bound for arbitrary bounded observation errors, even with the smooth true field $u=0$. It is separate from the missing derivative-regularity assumption. The corrected guarantee applies to normalized grid convolution at interior points when the kernel is resolved by the grid and the noise amplitude decreases sufficiently fast relative to the bandwidth.

checks.location: Appendix A.5 Eqs21-24, work/text/156782.txt:1125-1153, compared with Section3.2 kernel conditions
checks.claim: The A.5 alternatives are mollifying functions satisfying the main-text constraints of infinite differentiability, compact support and non-negativity, so analytic kernel derivatives can transfer arbitrary-order differentiation.
checks.explanation: The quartic is negative inside its support. The truncated polynomials have only finite boundary smoothness, and the sine and exponential formulas have nonzero boundary values for the listed radii below one. They therefore cannot all serve as nonnegative compact smooth kernels for arbitrary-order differentiation.
checks.demonstration:
Extend each displayed function by zero outside \((-R,R)\). The quadratic has

\[f_2(R)=0,\qquad f_2^{\prime}(R^-)=-2R,\qquad f_2^{\prime}(R^+)=0,\]

so it is not \(C^1\). The quartic obeys

\[f_4(0)=-R^4<0,\qquad f_4^{\prime\prime}(R^-)=-8R^2,\qquad f_4^{\prime\prime}(R^+)=0.\]

Its zero extension is \(C^1\) but not \(C^2\), and it is not nonnegative. For \(0<R<1\), the remaining boundary limits are

\[f_{\sin}(R^-)=\cos(\pi R^2/2)>0,\qquad f_{\exp}(R^-)=\exp[-1/(1-R^2)]>0,\]

so the literal zero extensions are discontinuous. Normalization changes neither these boundary jumps nor a polynomial’s finite smoothness. For instance, the normalized quadratic kernel \(k(x)=3(R^2-x^2)/(4R^3)\) on \((-R,R)\) preserves a constant under convolution, whose second derivative is zero. Integrating only its interior second derivative instead gives \(\int_{-R}^R k^{\prime\prime}(x)\,dx=-3/R^2\); the missing boundary distributions explain the discrepancy.
checks.repair:
For the smooth-kernel claims, use the normalized radius-scaled bump

\[\rho_R(x)=\begin{cases}c_R\exp[-1/(1-(x/R)^2)],&|x|<R,\\0,&|x|\ge R,\end{cases}\qquad c_R^{-1}=\int_{-R}^R\exp[-1/(1-(x/R)^2)]\,dx.\]

It is nonnegative, unit-mass and \(C^\infty\), with every derivative vanishing at the boundary. If polynomial alternatives are retained, correct the quartic sign and normalization, state their actual finite smoothness, and include boundary distributions for higher derivatives. The quadratic and sign-corrected quartic can support lower-order operations without being smooth all-order mollifiers.
checks.scope: The finding concerns the literal analytic kernel definitions and the class attributed to them. It does not invalidate the correctly assumed smooth kernel in Appendix A.8, or establish that high-order polynomial derivatives were used in the implementation. The first-order polynomial ablations do not themselves require arbitrary-order smoothness.
checks.title: The proposed kernel family does not share the stated smoothness and sign properties
checks.whyItMatters: When derivatives are transferred to a compact kernel, boundary regularity determines which analytic derivative formulas are valid.
checks.claimContext: Section 3.2 requires nonnegative, smooth, compactly supported mollifiers for transferring derivatives to the kernel. Appendix A.5 presents four functions on \((-R,R)\) as choices satisfying those constraints. Their literal zero extensions do not all belong to that class. The polynomial ablations are described as first-order; Appendix A.8 separately assumes a valid smooth normalized kernel.

checks.location: Appendix A.7 Eqs28-35, work/text/156782.txt:1212-1254, especially Eq33
checks.claim: For the eta_epsilon defined in Eqs28-30, f(x)-integral eta_epsilon(x-y)f(y)dy can be rewritten by subtracting f(y) from f(x) inside the kernel integral and tends to zero as epsilon shrinks.

checks.demonstration:
In one dimension, let \(M=\int_{-1}^1\eta(u)\,du>0\). At an interior point whose full kernel support lies in \(U\), change variables to obtain

\[\int_U\eta((x-y)/\epsilon)\,dy=\epsilon M.\]

For \(f\equiv1\), the left side of Equation (33) is \(|1-\epsilon M|\to1\), while its difference-integral right side is identically zero. In dimension \(n\), the unnormalized mass is similarly \(\epsilon^nM_n\). The contradiction uses a smooth constant and an interior point; it does not concern boundary treatment or the later derivative-rate assumptions.
checks.repair:
Define

\[\eta_\epsilon(t)=\frac{\eta(t/\epsilon)}{\epsilon^nM_n},\qquad M_n=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\eta(u)\,du.\]

The kernel then preserves constants, so Equation (33)’s difference-integral identity is valid wherever the full kernel window is included. For continuous \(f\), the error is bounded by its local modulus of continuity at radius \(\epsilon\), which tends to zero. This is the unit-mass convention already stated in Appendix A.8.
checks.scope: The correction repairs the local approximate-identity definition and proof in A.7. Appendix A.8 already normalizes its operator; this finding does not duplicate the separate derivative-regularity and noise-amplification errors in its quantitative theorem.

checks.location: Appendix A.4 Eq20 and minimum-learning-rate definition, work/text/156782.txt:1094-1121
checks.claim: The printed cosine schedule provides a smooth transition from the initial learning rate eta toward the defined minimum epsilon over the total training interval ending at T.
checks.explanation: The second branch starts above the initial rate and reaches a positive fraction of that rate at the final iteration, rather than the defined minimum.
checks.demonstration:
Assume \(0\le\epsilon<\eta\) and \(T>T_0\). At the join and endpoint, Equation (20) gives

\[\alpha_{T_0^-}=\eta,\qquad\alpha_{T_0}=\epsilon+\eta,\qquad\alpha_T=\epsilon+\eta\cos1.\]

Thus positive \(\epsilon\) creates a jump of size \(\epsilon\); even setting \(\epsilon=0\) leaves the endpoint at \(\eta\cos1\), not zero. For \(\eta=10^{-3}\) and \(\epsilon=10^{-6}\), the final value is approximately \(5.4130\times10^{-4}\), rather than \(10^{-6}\).
checks.repair:
Use the constant first branch and replace the second by

\[\alpha_t=\epsilon+\frac{\eta-\epsilon}{2}\left[1+\cos\!\left(\pi\frac{t-T_0}{T-T_0}\right)\right],\qquad T_0\le t\le T.\]

It equals \(\eta\) at \(T_0\), equals \(\epsilon\) at \(T\), and has zero slope at both endpoints. Its derivative is nonpositive throughout that interval, proving the intended smooth decrease.
